extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans and researchers interested in the BBC comedy panel show QI
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative standards and production/Editorial criteria that the QI Wikipedia page implies or states for a British television comedy panel show (QI). Focuses on content interestingness, tone, sensitivity, diversity, commercial tie-ins and related measures of quality/success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interestingness (programme philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whatever is interesting we are interested in. Whatever is not interesting, we are even more interested in. Everything is interesting if looked at in the right way.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: QI's central criterion is that content must be 'quite interesting' — select facts, questions and topics that provoke curiosity. The programme explicitly prioritises unusual, counter‑intuitive or overlooked material; being 'interesting' (including finding interest in things usually considered uninteresting) is the organising standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone balance: intellectual seriousness vs silliness
rubrics_metrics.description: The show ranges from "serious, intensely scientific, deeply mystical" to "hilarious, silly and frothy enough to please the most indolent couch‑potato."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a balance between cerebral content and light, silly humour — episodes may swing toward either extreme but should allow both intellectual exploration and broad laughs. Both extremes are presented as acceptable facets of the show's identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host/panellist quality: brainy and articulate presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics praise Stephen Fry as 'brainy and articulate' and the show benefits from an articulate, intelligent host and witty panellists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hosts and guests should combine intelligence, articulation and comedic skill — able to be 'scathing and generous' — because that delivery is repeatedly cited as central to the show's appeal. Poorly informed or inarticulate presentation is an anti‑pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational, familiar atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The show makes viewers feel 'like you're at the pub with the funny, clever people' — a sense of easy familiarity and casual pontification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for an intimate, conversational style rather than distant or heavily staged performance; the tone should draw viewers in through informal banter and rapport among participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing comedians to be clever (not dumbed‑down)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers note QI as 'one of the last truly popular programmes on mainstream television where comedians are allowed to be clever' in contrast to 'dumbed‑down' schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content and jokes should reward intelligence and wit rather than relying on lowest‑common‑denominator humour. Avoid simplifying material to the point that cleverness is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational/informational value
rubrics_metrics.description: The show is described as 'funny, educational, and ... quite interesting'; books and segments emphasise factual clarifications and lists (e.g., 'General Ignorance' misconceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine humour with accurate, well‑researched facts and insights. Educational payoff (new or counterintuitive information) is a core measure of success and audience value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format originality and question design
rubrics_metrics.description: The programme uses unconventional trivia elements (e.g., 'General Ignorance' rounds, unanswerable questions) and distinctive recurring features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rounds and questions that subvert expectations, reward lateral thinking, or expose popular misconceptions. Originality in format and question construction is a positive criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy and willingness to correct
rubrics_metrics.description: Book editions were revised to 'corrected and updated some of the information' and added new sections; many facts and clarifications appeared on the programme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain high standards of factual accuracy in both broadcast and ancillary publications; issue corrections and updated editions when necessary. Failure to correct errors is an anti‑pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to offensive subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurrences (atomic bomb jokes about Tsutomu Yamaguchi, limerick about paedophilia, remarks about Margaret Thatcher) led to complaints and a BBC apology acknowledging 'the sensitivity of the subject matter'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of historical tragedies, recent deaths, and subjects likely to cause harm to specific groups or individuals. Avoid punchlines that trivialise serious suffering; when offence occurs, broadcaster guidelines and audience sentiment should guide responses (apologies, edits, postponements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with broadcaster/editorial guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC Trust described an incident as 'capable of causing offence' but not in breach of guidelines; BBC issued apology recognizing sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure material complies with network editorial standards and review processes. Even when content is permitted under guidelines, consider reputational risks and audience sensitivity; prepare justifications or corrections where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest selection and diversity (gender balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics showed low female representation (30.1% rising to 31.9%); BBC later banned all‑male panels on comedy shows and the show faced criticism about lack of women guests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively include women and underrepresented groups among panellists to avoid all‑male lineups; diversity in casting is a stated standard and a public expectation. Tokenism should be avoided; meaningful inclusion is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/avoidance of amplifying controversial publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: An episode featuring Jeremy Clarkson was postponed due to recent controversial comments he had made; the decision aimed 'to avoid putting Clarkson in the spotlight.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about booking or airing episodes when a guest is the centre of recent negative publicity; consider postponement or editorial adjustments to avoid amplifying controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience/popularity as success metric
rubrics_metrics.description: QI was 'the most popular programme on BBC Four in 2005' and routinely drew millions of viewers across episodes and series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratings and audience figures are used to assess success; sustained or increasing viewership and strong reception indicate programme health. Low ratings are a negative signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception criteria (wit, charm, format chemistry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics highlighted traits like 'tweedy goodness, cockney charm, pub trivia and class war' and praised the chemistry of Fry and Alan Davies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate shows on comic chemistry among participants, balance of cultural sensibilities (e.g., wit and charm), and the way format elements (trivia, banter) are combined. Lack of chemistry or flattening of distinctive tone weakens critical reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross‑media expansion and tie‑ins
rubrics_metrics.description: QI expanded into bestselling books (The Book of General Ignorance), DVDs, columns, magazine features, online shows and a website with facts and forums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage successful formats into books, online content, columns and merchandise to extend brand reach. Quality of tie‑ins (accuracy, additive content) reflects on the core property; tie‑ins that duplicate low‑quality content are anti‑patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release quality for home media (extras and completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: DVD releases included outtakes, the unbroadcast pilot, 'Factoids' features and other extras; later complete series box sets contained 'making of' features, interviews and bloopers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Home media should include value‑added extras (outtakes, interviews, making‑of) and ideally present complete, well‑packaged series. Omitting desirable extras or releasing incomplete sets can disappoint core fans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights/clearance management for distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2014 note cited 'a number of copyright issues' making it difficult to release further series on DVD; distribution deals later resolved availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively manage music, clip and rights clearances to ensure ongoing availability on DVD/streaming. Poor rights planning delays releases and limits audience access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a dedicated research team and sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: QI credits a head of research and 'The QI Elves'; many facts and clarifications derive from that research function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a research team to source, verify and curate material; reliable research underpins the show's factual and educational value. Lack of research resources risks factual errors and weaker content.
